name: Spiky anime-style false lashes

card.summary: Dramatic clustered false eyelashes with a spiky, doll-like look, used in gyaru makeup to make the eyes appear larger and more defined.
card.aka: anime lashes; gyaru lashes; spiky lashes
card.note: Glued-on lashes are temporary and are not meant to be worn in the shower, while sleeping or swimming.

quick.overview:
Spiky or anime-style false lashes are bold lash strips or clusters that read as separated, pointed spikes rather than a soft, wispy fan. They come from gyaru makeup in Japan, where dramatic lashes on both the upper and lower lids are a defining feature of the look.

They help someone look like they have larger, more defined, doll-like eyes when worn, and the effect is temporary. The style is a fashion choice and is discussed in fashion and makeup writing rather than in clinical research.
quick.how: Strip lashes are trimmed to fit and attached above the natural lash line with lash adhesive, then removed with warm water or makeup remover. Lower-lid lashes are applied in the gyaru style as well. Magnetic and extension versions exist for other lash looks.
quick.risks: Adhesives and removal can irritate the eyelids, and lashes are advised against for sleeping, showering or swimming. Reactions to glue are a known issue with any false lashes.

lead: Spiky or anime-style false eyelashes are exaggerated lashes that appear as clustered, separated points rather than a natural fan. In the gyaru fashion subculture of Japan, a typical early-2010s look combined matte foundation, dark lash lines, colored or circle contacts and dramatic false lashes, which were described as spiky or anime-style with a clustered rather than wispy appearance and applied to both upper and lower lids [2].

People wear them to make the eyes look bigger and more doll-like, as part of a complete makeup look that also includes downward-curved eyeliner. Gyaru style has since become more varied, with lighter makeup, smaller lashes and thinner liner in the Reiwa era, and social media has largely replaced print magazines as the source of trends [2].

False lashes in general have a long history: a patent for artificial lashes in the UK in 1902, a crescent-shaped strip patented in the US in 1911, and widespread popularity in the 1930s and 1960s [1]. No clinical studies address the anime-lash style.

chain: Dramatic lash strip applied along the lash line
Eyes look larger and more outlined
angle.text: The lashes add visible length and density immediately, with a stylized spiky shape. The effect lasts until they are removed.

paras: Gyaru is a Japanese fashion subculture, with roots in the 1970s use of "gal" and a heyday in the 1990s and 2000s through kogal and ganguro styles; it declined in the 2010s and diversified later [2]. Within gyaru makeup, dramatic false lashes were central [2].

Temporary strip lashes are trimmed and glued above the natural lashes; magnetic lashes sandwich the natural lashes with a magnetic strip and were invented in 2014; extensions are applied individually by technicians and last roughly three to four weeks [1].
False lashes are designed not to be worn when showering, sleeping or swimming, and US states may regulate extensions through cosmetology or esthetician licensing [1].

timeline.event: Karl Nessler patents artificial eyelashes in the UK [1].
Anna Taylor patents a crescent-shaped lash strip in the US [1].
Magnetic lashes are invented as a glue-free alternative [1].
